'''Isurugihiko Shrine''' (伊須流岐比古神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} located at the summit of {{ill|Mount Sekidō|en|Mount Sekidō|qid=Q11585200|lt=Mount Isurugi}} (Ōmimae) in {{ill|Nakanoto, Ishikawa|ar|ناكانوتو|arz|ناكانوتو|ceb|Nakanoto Machi|es|Nakanoto (Ishikawa)|fa|ناکانوتو|fr|Nakanoto|it|Nakanoto|ja|中能登町|ko|나카노토정|ms|Nakanoto, Ishikawa|my|နခနိုတိုမြို့၊ အိရှိခါဝါ|nl|Nakanoto|pl|Nakanoto|ru|Наканото|sv|Nakanoto|tl|Nakanoto, Ishikawa|tr|Nakanoto|uk|Нака-Ното|ur|ناکانوٹو، ایشیکاوا|vi|Nakanoto, Ishikawa|zh|中能登町|qid=Q1349436|lt=Nakanoto, Ishikawa}}, {{ill|Kashima District, Ishikawa|ceb|Kashima Gun|es|Distrito de Kashima (Ishikawa)|fr|District de Kashima|id|Distrik Kashima, Ishikawa|it|Distretto di Kashima|ja|鹿島郡|ko|가시마군|pl|Powiat Kashima (Ishikawa)|uk|Повіт Касіма (Ісікава)|zh|鹿島郡|qid=Q1130967|lt=Kashima District, Ishikawa}}, {{ill|Ishikawa Prefecture|en|Ishikawa Prefecture|qid=Q131281|lt=Ishikawa Prefecture}}. It is also written as '''Isurugihiko Shrine''' (伊須留岐比古神社) and is the second-Ranked shrine (二宮) of {{ill|Noto Province|en|Noto Province|qid=Q1047671|lt=Noto Province}}.

== Deities ==
The shrine enshrines {{ill|Isurugihiko-no-Kami|ja|伊須流岐比古神|qid=Q140446114}} (also known as Ishurugi-hiko) and {{ill|Kikurihime|ja|白山比咩神|lt=Hakusan-Hime-no-Kami}}.

Among them, the main deity, Isurugihiko-no-Kami, appears in the ''Kōkō Sentatsu Roku'' (肯構泉達録) and other sources as a He is also identified with {{ill|Isurugi Gongen|ja|石動権現}}, one of the {{ill|Gosha Gongen|ja|五社権現|qid=Q140446113}}. The ancient name of Mount Isurugi, "Isurugi" or "Yusurugi," means "a mountain where stones move," which is thought to originate from Daoist star worship and influences from {{ill|Shugendō|en|Shugendō|qid=Q1483875|lt=Shugendō}}, as well as the legend of a divine stone that descended from the heavens.<ref name="kobayashi" /> This stone was said to tremble and manifest divine power. The shrine was founded to pacify the trembling stone and enshrine it as a deity.

During the Meiji period's {{ill|State Shinto|bn|রাষ্ট্রীয় শিন্তৌ|de|Staats-Shintō|es|Sintoísmo estatal|fa|شینتوی حکومتی|fr|Shintoïsme d'État|id|Shinto Negara|ja|国家神道|ko|국가신토|no|Statsshinto|pt|Xintoísmo estatal|ru|Государственный синтоизм|simple|State Shinto|tr|Devlet Şintoizmi|vi|Thần đạo Quốc gia|zh|国家神道|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto}}, the name "Gongen" was rejected, and the deity is now called Isurugihiko-no-Kami or Ishurugi-hiko.

{{ill|Kikurihime|ja|白山比咩神|lt=Hakusan-Hime-no-Kami}} is also enshrined as an {{ill|Aiden-shin|ja|相殿|fr|Saijin|lt=Aiden-shin}} deity. Additionally, Ishurugi-hiko and Hakusan-Hime-no-Kami have been associated with {{ill|Izanagi|en|Izanagi|qid=Q813858|lt=Izanagi}} and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|qid=Q682306|lt=Izanami}}. The shrine's historical Buddhist counterpart deities (本地仏) were {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|en|Ākāśagarbha|qid=Q416174|lt=Kokūzō Bosatsu}} (for Isurugihiko-no-Kami) and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|en|Ekādaśamukha|qid=Q11404731|lt=Eleven-Headed Kannon}} (for Hakusan-Hime-no-Kami).

== History ==
Since ancient times, a shrine has existed on Mount Isurugi (Ōmimae), worshipped by fishermen and farmers. This shrine is identified with the ''Isurugihiko Shrine'' mentioned in the {{ill|Engishiki|en|Engishiki|qid=Q1342448|lt=Engishiki}}'s list of shrines.<ref name="kobayashi" /> It is one of the {{ill|Shikinaisha|ja|式内社|lt=Shikinaisha}} recorded in the ''Engishiki''.

According to the ''Isurugi-san Koyengi'' (石動山古縁起), the mountain was opened by the hermit {{ill|Hōdō Sennin|ja|方道仙人}} in the 6th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|qid=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin}}, and in 717, the monk Chitoku Shōnin ascended the mountain and built the Great Ritual Hall (講堂) in 756 (''Tenpyō Shōhō'' 8).<ref name="kobayashi">{{Cite journal|和書|author=小林忠雄 |date=1996-03 |url=https://doi.org/10.15024/00000767 |title=都市空間の原初形態 : 山岳寺院の構造と広場性 |journal=国立歴史民俗博物館研究報告 |ISSN=0286-7400 |publisher=国立歴史民俗博物館 |volume=67 |pages=95-136 |doi=10.15024/00000767 |naid=120005748043}}</ref> Alternatively, a long-standing tradition attributes the shrine's founding to {{ill|Taichō|en|Taichō|qid=Q2388439|lt=Taichō}}, and the ''Shin Engi'' written by {{ill|Hayashi Razan|en|Hayashi Razan|qid=Q558279|lt=Hayashi Razan}} in the early modern period also attributes its establishment to Taichō.<ref name="kobayashi" />

In the {{ill|Kamakura period|ar|فترة كاماكورا|be|Перыяд Камакура|bg|Камакура|bn|কামাকুরা যুগ|ckb|سەردەمی کاماکورا|cs|Období Kamakura|de|Kamakura-Zeit|eo|Kamakura-epoko|es|Período Kamakura|et|Kamakura ajastu|eu|Kamakura aroa|fa|دوره کاماکورا|fi|Kamakura-kausi|fr|Époque de Kamakura|gl|Período Kamakura|he|תקופת קמקורה|hu|Kamakura-kor|id|Zaman Kamakura|it|Periodo Kamakura|ja|鎌倉時代|ko|가마쿠라 시대|lt|Kamakura laikotarpis|mn|Камакура эрин|nl|Kamakuraperiode|no|Kamakura-perioden|pt|Período Kamakura|ru|Период Камакура|simple|Kamakura period|sk|Obdobie Kamakura|sl|Obdobje Kamakura|sr|Камакура период|sv|Kamakura|th|ยุคคามากูระ|tl|Panahong Kamakura|tr|Kamakura Dönemi|uk|Період Камакура|vi|Thời kỳ Kamakura|wuu|镰仓时代|zh|鎌倉時代|zh_min_nan|Kamakura sî-tāi|zh_yue|鎌倉時代|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}, Shingon monks constructed temple buildings, leading to the shrine being called "Isurugi Temple" (石動寺) under the {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|Shinbutsu-shūgō|qid=Q2279088|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} system. It became a major religious center, boasting over 360 temple lodges and around 3,000 monks.<ref name="kobayashi" />

However, according to the ''Taiheiki'', during the {{ill|Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)|en|Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)|qid=Q8140349|lt=Nanboku-chō period}}, the temple supported the Southern Court and was burned down by enemy forces (First Battle of Mount Isurugi).<ref name="kobayashi" /> It was later rebuilt under the patronage of the Ashikaga shogunate and became a subsidiary of {{ill|Kajū-ji|en|Kajū-ji|qid=Q772598|lt=Kanjū-ji}}, adopting the name ''Tenpyō-ji''.<ref name="kobayashi" />

In 1582, the shrine was again burned down when the monks sided with Noto loyalists against {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|en|Oda Nobunaga|qid=Q171411|lt=Oda Nobunaga}}'s forces (Second Battle of Mount Isurugi, {{ill|Arayama Battle|ja|荒山合戦|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q28683115}}).<ref name="kobayashi" />

The current main shrine was built in 1653 by {{ill|Maeda Toshitsune|en|Maeda Toshitsune|qid=Q587204|lt=Maeda Toshitsune}} of the {{ill|Kaga Domain|en|Kaga Domain|qid=Q903448|lt=Kaga Domain}} and was originally called "Ōmiya."
